title: Two Ways to Start, Several Ways to Stop

scenes.tts: The first film followed strand choice into a growing RNA. Why do bacteria and nuclei use different teams to start that same reaction? Keep watching the promoter. The team assembled there decides where polymerase begins, and in the nucleus, which polymerase.
scenes.caption: The first film followed strand choice into a growing RNA. Why do bacteria and nuclei use different teams to start that same reaction? Keep watching the promoter. The team assembled there decides where polymerase begins, and in the nucleus, which polymerase.
scenes.visual: Reuse the first film's COLOR MAP exactly: template DNA blue, coding DNA gold, RNA green, promoter teal, polymerase white. The carried schematic duplex and promoter split into an E. coli lane and a nucleus lane. Different empty docking outlines pulse over the same start marker.
scenes.narration: The first film followed strand choice into a growing RNA. Why do bacteria and nuclei use different teams to start that same reaction? Keep watching the promoter. The team assembled there decides where polymerase begins, and in the nucleus, which polymerase.

scenes.visual: The two lanes narrow beneath the centered title 'Two Ways to Start, Several Ways to Stop'. Hold only the title and lanes for two seconds, then expand both lanes to fill the frame.

scenes.tts: Both systems must solve the same physical jobs. They must recognize a promoter, place polymerase, open DNA, and start RNA. After productive synthesis, they must release the RNA and polymerase. The parts differ, but those jobs remain.
scenes.caption: Both systems must solve the same physical jobs. They must recognize a promoter, place polymerase, open DNA, and start RNA. After productive synthesis, they must release the RNA and polymerase. The parts differ, but those jobs remain.
scenes.visual: Across both lanes, four large action icons transform in sequence: teal promoter recognition, white polymerase placement, opening blue-gold bubble, growing green RNA. The track extends to a final release icon, all marked 'schematic'.
scenes.narration: Both systems must solve the same physical jobs. They must recognize a promoter, place polymerase, open DNA, and start RNA. After productive synthesis, they must release the RNA and polymerase. The parts differ, but those jobs remain.

scenes.tts: In E. coli, core polymerase performs nearly all cellular transcription. Core can join RNA nucleotides, but it finds promoters poorly. A sigma factor docks onto core, forming holoenzyme. Sigma recognizes promoter elements and positions the active site over the start.
scenes.caption: In E. coli, core polymerase performs nearly all cellular transcription. Core can join RNA nucleotides, but it finds promoters poorly. A sigma factor docks onto core, forming holoenzyme. Sigma recognizes promoter elements and positions the active site over the start.
scenes.visual: In the bacterial lane, a white core block moves past several teal promoter blocks without locking. A violet sigma key docks onto core; the combined holoenzyme now fits one promoter outline and settles over the start marker.
scenes.narration: In E. coli, core polymerase performs nearly all cellular transcription. Core can join RNA nucleotides, but it finds promoters poorly. A sigma factor docks onto core, forming holoenzyme. Sigma recognizes promoter elements and positions the active site over the start.

scenes.tts: Imagine removing sigma while leaving core intact. Which ability fails most directly: joining RNA nucleotides, or starting accurately at promoters?
scenes.caption: Imagine removing sigma while leaving core intact. Which ability fails most directly: joining RNA nucleotides, or starting accurately at promoters?
scenes.visual: Detach violet sigma from the white core. Place two large choices beside the carried bacterial lane: a green growing-RNA icon and a teal target-start icon. Both pulse neutrally while the question remains visible.
scenes.narration: Imagine removing sigma while leaving core intact. Which ability fails most directly: joining RNA nucleotides, or starting accurately at promoters?

scenes.visual: Keep the core, detached sigma and both choices visible. Slowly drift core past the promoter without locking, but do not highlight either answer during the thinking pause.

scenes.tts: Accurate starting fails. Core remains catalytically capable, yet it chooses promoter starts poorly. Restore sigma, and the holoenzyme forms a closed complex. DNA then opens around the start. Short RNAs may be released before polymerase escapes into elongation.
scenes.caption: Accurate starting fails. Core remains catalytically capable, yet it chooses promoter starts poorly. Restore sigma, and the holoenzyme forms a closed complex. DNA then opens around the start. Short RNAs may be released before polymerase escapes into elongation.
scenes.visual: Highlight the teal target-start choice, not the RNA-joining choice. Redock sigma. The holoenzyme clamps closed DNA, opens the carried bubble, releases several tiny green RNA tiles, then moves downstream with one growing RNA.
scenes.narration: Accurate starting fails. Core remains catalytically capable, yet it chooses promoter starts poorly. Restore sigma, and the holoenzyme forms a closed complex. DNA then opens around the start. Short RNAs may be released before polymerase escapes into elongation.

scenes.tts: A eukaryotic nucleus divides transcription among its main polymerases. Polymerase one makes the large ribosomal RNA precursor. Polymerase two makes messenger RNA precursors, most small nuclear RNAs, and microRNA precursors. Polymerase three makes transfer RNAs, a separate ribosomal RNA, and other small RNAs.
scenes.caption: A eukaryotic nucleus divides transcription among its main polymerases. Pol I makes the large rRNA precursor. Pol II makes mRNA precursors, most snRNAs, and microRNA precursors. Pol III makes tRNAs, a separate rRNA, and other small RNAs.
scenes.visual: In the nucleus lane, one white polymerase block transforms into three labeled blocks: Pol I, Pol II and Pol III. Green RNA ribbons flow to three product bins labeled 'large rRNA precursor', 'mRNA precursors, snRNAs, miRNA precursors', and 'tRNAs, 5S rRNA, small RNAs'.
scenes.narration: A eukaryotic nucleus divides transcription among its main polymerases. Pol I makes the large rRNA precursor. Pol II makes mRNA precursors, most snRNAs, and microRNA precursors. Pol III makes tRNAs, a separate rRNA, and other small RNAs.

scenes.tts: Follow polymerase two, the enzyme that makes messenger RNA precursors. General transcription factors assemble at its core promoter. Some recognize promoter DNA. Others position polymerase and help open the template. The classic sequence is useful, although living complexes exchange parts rapidly.
scenes.caption: Follow Pol II, the enzyme that makes mRNA precursors. General transcription factors assemble at its core promoter. Some recognize promoter DNA. Others position polymerase and help open the template. The classic sequence is useful, although living complexes exchange parts rapidly.
scenes.visual: Enlarge the Pol II lane. Several distinct factor blocks arrive and build a platform on the teal promoter; use generic labels 'recognize', 'position', and 'open', not named factors. The white Pol II block settles into the platform as the blue template enters its slot.
scenes.narration: Follow Pol II, the enzyme that makes mRNA precursors. General transcription factors assemble at its core promoter. Some recognize promoter DNA. Others position polymerase and help open the template. The classic sequence is useful, although living complexes exchange parts rapidly.

scenes.tts: Both lanes now converge on the same motion. DNA opens, a green RNA begins, and polymerase escapes the promoter. The first film's direction rule still applies. Different proteins chose the start, but chemistry fixes how the RNA grows.
scenes.caption: Both lanes now converge on the same motion. DNA opens, a green RNA begins, and polymerase escapes the promoter. The first film's direction rule still applies. Different proteins chose the start, but chemistry fixes how the RNA grows.
scenes.visual: Synchronize both lanes. Their bubbles open together, green RNAs begin, and white polymerases move downstream. Merge the lanes into one carried elongation track while preserving blue template, gold coding strand and green RNA.
scenes.narration: Both lanes now converge on the same motion. DNA opens, a green RNA begins, and polymerase escapes the promoter. The first film's direction rule still applies. Different proteins chose the start, but chemistry fixes how the RNA grows.

scenes.tts: Bacteria can end transcription through different routes. In one, the RNA folds into a hairpin followed by a U rich tract. Together they destabilize the complex. In another, Rho binds the RNA, advances toward polymerase, and promotes release.
scenes.caption: Bacteria can end transcription through different routes. In one, the RNA folds into a hairpin followed by a U-rich tract. Together they destabilize the complex. In another, Rho binds the RNA, advances toward polymerase, and promotes release.
scenes.visual: Split the elongation track. On one schematic branch, the green RNA bends into a simple hairpin icon beside a labeled U-rich strip and the complex loosens. On the other, a violet Rho ring advances along green RNA toward polymerase; avoid showing atomic structure.
scenes.narration: Bacteria can end transcription through different routes. In one, the RNA folds into a hairpin followed by a U-rich tract. Together they destabilize the complex. In another, Rho binds the RNA, advances toward polymerase, and promotes release.

scenes.tts: Polymerase two couples termination to RNA processing. After it copies a polyadenylation signal, the RNA is cut. A following enzyme degrades the attached RNA toward polymerase. Evidence supports this pursuit working with changes that make polymerase ready to stop.
scenes.caption: Pol II couples termination to RNA processing. After it copies a poly(A) signal, the RNA is cut. A following enzyme degrades the attached RNA toward polymerase. Evidence supports this pursuit working with changes that make polymerase ready to stop.
scenes.visual: Return to the Pol II track. A teal poly(A) signal block passes through polymerase. The green RNA is cut downstream; an orange follower advances along the attached RNA while the white polymerase gradually slows. Label the combined picture 'supported model, schematic'.
scenes.narration: Pol II couples termination to RNA processing. After it copies a poly(A) signal, the RNA is cut. A following enzyme degrades the attached RNA toward polymerase. Evidence supports this pursuit working with changes that make polymerase ready to stop.

scenes.tts: Starting and stopping are therefore separate control problems. Initiation machinery chooses a usable start and places the enzyme. Termination signals and factors destabilize or remodel the elongation complex. Between them, polymerase carries out the same directional chemistry.
scenes.caption: Starting and stopping are therefore separate control problems. Initiation machinery chooses a usable start and places the enzyme. Termination signals and factors destabilize or remodel the elongation complex. Between them, polymerase carries out the same directional chemistry.
scenes.visual: Compress the full journey into one wide track: teal start gate, moving white polymerase with green RNA, and a release gate. Bacterial and nuclear initiation-team blocks hover above the start; several hedged termination-route icons hover above release.
scenes.narration: Starting and stopping are therefore separate control problems. Initiation machinery chooses a usable start and places the enzyme. Termination signals and factors destabilize or remodel the elongation complex. Between them, polymerase carries out the same directional chemistry.

scenes.visual: Show one centered line only: 'Different initiation teams place polymerase; termination releases RNA and enzyme.' No logo, subtitle, URL, second line, or smaller text.
